verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface, and granular access controls can be implemented across all secrets.
verdicts.evidence: For ESC, the docs landing page lists a CLI ("Pulumi CLI … Command-line interface for managing environments, secrets, and configuration"), SDKs ("Use the ESC SDKs to retrieve environment values…" for Node.js, Python, Go and .NET) and an editor interface. The Vault half (vault CLI, client libraries, web UI, ACL policies) is well-known product behavior, but I didn't fetch a Vault source to back it this session.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Granular access controls across all secrets" is broad marketing phrasing. ESC RBAC works at the environment level, not on individual secrets.

verdicts.text: Vault is not open source; it uses the Business Source License model.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's upstream LICENSE file confirms the claim: it reads "Business Source License 1.1" and "Licensed Work: Vault Version 1.15.0 or later". BSL is source-available but not an OSI-approved open source license, so "not open source" holds for current Vault. One caveat: releases before 1.15 were MPL 2.0, and each BSL version switches to MPL 2.0 four years after it is published.
verdicts.framing_note: Holds for current Vault (1.15.0 and later); older versions were open source under MPL 2.0. The licensor is now listed as IBM.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc repo is licensed Apache-2.0 (the GitHub API returns `Apache-2.0`), so the license claim is correct. "Fully open source" goes too far, though. The repo contains the CLI and evaluation engine, while the ESC service itself runs in Pulumi Cloud, which is not open source. The same page (L52) calls ESC a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud".
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc (license.spdx_id: Apache-2.0); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L27, L46-52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the open-source 'pulumi/esc' repo (CLI/engine, Apache-2.0) becomes 'ESC is fully open source', but the hosted ESC service in Pulumi Cloud is proprietary
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Fully open source" sits awkwardly next to the page's own description of ESC as a Pulumi Cloud SaaS service

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration."

verdicts.text: Through Pulumi ESC, secrets stored in Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't check this independently. The only support I found is the reviewed page itself, which can't count as evidence. Its table says environments "can be versioned and tagged" and "forked for testing". My guesses at the ESC versioning and Vault integration doc paths didn't exist, and GitHub code search hit rate limits (HTTP 429). ESC versioning, and composition through imports, are well-known features. Native "branching" of environments is not something I could confirm.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L31, L95, L120 (reviewed file only, so not independent); gh search code returned HTTP 429
verdicts.intuition_flag: "branched" may overstate ESC. As far as I know, ESC has versions, tags and imports but no native branch primitive; the page's own table says "forked", which may just mean cloning or overriding.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is open source under Apache License 2.0, while Vault is not open source and uses Business Source License 1.1.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub license API returns `Apache-2.0` for pulumi/esc. For hashicorp/vault it returns `NOASSERTION Other`, meaning the license is not a recognized open-source SPDX license. That fits HashiCorp's 2023 move to BSL 1.1, but I couldn't read the Vault LICENSE text itself to confirm "1.1" (base64 decode was blocked, then rate-limited).
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/license; gh api repos/hashicorp/vault/license

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is a fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC get-started docs back this up: "Pulumi ESC ... is a centralized secrets and configuration management service that is part of Pulumi Cloud". They also say "ESC requires the Pulumi Cloud backend." That shows ESC is delivered as a Pulumi Cloud service. The docs don't use the words "fully managed" themselves.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi Cloud also comes in a self-hosted edition. If ESC ships with it, "fully managed SaaS" leaves out that self-hosting option, which is the same thing this table points out about Vault.

verdicts.text: Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp docs confirm "HCP Vault Dedicated is a hosted version of Vault Enterprise operated by HashiCorp", and self-hosted Vault Enterprise/Community editions exist too. "Significant management overhead" is an opinion, but third-party sources back it up: running Vault in production means managing storage backends, unseal keys, replication, upgrades, and disaster recovery.
verdicts.intuition_flag: HCP Vault Secrets (the lightweight SaaS) reached end of life on July 1, 2026, so HCP Vault Dedicated is now the only hosted option. The claim still holds, but any nearby text that mentions HCP Vault Secrets is out of date.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide a key-value store.
verdicts.evidence: The claim holds for both products. ESC environments store static named values under a `values:` map ("This defines two values: `region` (a plaintext value) and `apiKey` (a secret value…)"). For Vault, the pulumi-vault provider ships a `kv` module (`kv/secretV2.ts`, `secretBackendV2.ts`) that wraps Vault's KV secrets engine.
verdicts.framing_note: ESC docs don't use the phrase "key-value store"; its storage of named values as key-value pairs comes from the environment YAML structure.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports pulling and using secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC docs overview (a different page from the one under review) says ESC can "pull and synchronize secrets and configuration data, including AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, and 1Password." ESC also has provider pages for 1password-secrets and vault-secrets.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names no source. The corroboration comes from Pulumi's own docs pages (the reference page is auto-generated from the ESC API schema), which match the claim's list of providers.

verdicts.text: Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault (no open ecosystem of external secret sources).
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say some Vault secrets engines only store and read data, but "Other secrets engines connect to other services and generate dynamic credentials on demand." Its validated design says dynamic roles "manage the full lifecycle of credentials in external systems" (AWS, Azure, databases). That makes "can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault" too absolute. The narrower point may still hold: Vault does not pull secrets from other secret stores such as AWS Secrets Manager the way ESC does.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is marketing copy on a competitor-comparison page. "Can only" overstates the case: Vault's dynamic secrets engines and Secrets Sync both work with external systems. A better wording would be "does not pull secrets from external secret stores."

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's ESC editor-enhancements post describes "Auto-complete", "Enhanced Diagnostics... as-you-type insights into errors", and "Hover Documentation" for the ESC environment editor. Release Notes 103, titled "Pulumi ESC Table Editor", announce both the table (GUI) editor and the YAML editor upgrades, which covers the "both a GUI and a Document Editor" part of the claim.
verdicts.framing_note: Both sources are Pulumi's own blog posts, not product source. They back the claim but can't settle it independently, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: Vault's editing experience is limited: it offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV v2 tutorial confirms the UI has a key/value pair form with a JSON toggle: "Notice the JSON toggle in the UI. Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." Calling it "limited" is a subjective comparison, and it lines up with a user's feature request (#6909) saying the JSON view is just a plain text box.
verdicts.framing_note: The factual part (a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle) is confirmed. "Limited" is the author's own comparative judgment.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference, built from pulumi/pulumi, documents `pulumi env` ("Manage environments"). Its subcommands include `pulumi env run`, "Open the environment with the given name and run a command.", which is how secrets get injected as environment variables. They also include `pulumi env set` ("Set a value within an environment."), `edit`, and `rotate` for changing secrets.

verdicts.text: The `vault` CLI reads and writes secrets but does not inject them as environment variables.
verdicts.evidence: In HashiCorp's docs, injecting secrets as environment variables is a Vault Agent feature (process supervisor mode), not something the read/write CLI commands like `vault kv get`/`put` do: "Vault Agent will inject secrets referenced in the env_template configuration blocks as environment variables into the child process specified in the exec block." So the claim holds if "vault CLI" means the read/write commands and Vault Agent is treated as a separate tool.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Agent runs from the same binary as `vault agent` (process supervisor mode, Vault 1.14+). If the page doesn't name Vault Agent as the tool that does env injection, saying "the vault CLI does not inject" is misleading.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault have client SDKs.
verdicts.evidence: The public repo pulumi/esc-sdk exists, so Pulumi ESC does have a client SDK. HashiCorp Vault's client libraries (for example vault-client-go) are well known, but I couldn't check them in this lane because gh is limited to pulumi-owned repos.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi → pulumi/esc-sdk

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows managing (create, update, delete) collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice provider has a `pulumiservice:Environment` resource. Its YAML example declares an ESC environment through the `organization`, `project`, `name` and `yaml` (values) properties. That means ESC environments can be created, updated and deleted as infrastructure-as-code resources.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." That backs the claim that environments inherit values from the environments they import.

verdicts.text: Vault has no equivalent concept to composable environments; secrets are organized by path convention and the structure is maintained by hand.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Vault KV lets you store key-value pairs "at any nested path, allowing to reflect organizational or logical structure". None of the Vault docs or tutorials returned show a native way for one secret path to import, merge, or layer another. Vault Enterprise namespaces do inherit policies, but that governs access control, not composition of config values. So the claim holds in substance, but it's an absolute negative that's hard to prove.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault KV secrets path organization inheritance composition"; https://dev.to/admantium/hashicorp-vault-cli-part-8-secrets-management-and-key-value-engine-153g; https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/enterprise/namespaces/namespace-structure
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Maintained by hand" is loaded wording: many teams manage Vault path structure with Terraform or other IaC. Also, Vault Enterprise namespaces and templated policies give some hierarchy, though not value composition.

verdicts.text: Vault secrets are individually versioned, which is a limited form of versioning.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp docs say versioning happens per key: "When running v2 of the kv secrets engine, a key can retain a configurable number of versions," and `max_versions` is "The number of versions to keep per key." So the fact that Vault versions secrets one at a time checks out. Calling that "limited" is the page's own opinion, comparing it with ESC's versioning of whole environments.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Only the KV v2 engine versions secrets. KV v1 and dynamic secrets have no versioning at all, so "Vault secrets" slightly overgeneralizes.

verdicts.text: Vault values can only be secrets, not plaintext, whereas Pulumi ESC values can be secret or plaintext.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say the KV engine stores "arbitrary secrets" and that "Secrets written to Vault are encrypted and then written to backend storage". Vault has no separate type for unencrypted config values. ESC does: "Any value wrapped in fn::secret is encrypted at rest", while a value like `region: us-west-2` is marked plaintext configuration.
verdicts.framing_note: Vault still returns stored values in plaintext on read (vault kv get). The claim is right if "plaintext" means an unencrypted, non-secret value type, but a reader could take it to mean Vault never shows plaintext.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Can only be secrets, not plaintext" is loose wording. It could be misread as a claim about how values are displayed, rather than about the value type or encryption at rest.

verdicts.text: Vault does not provide the ability to see existing secrets, whereas Pulumi ESC does.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs show that Vault lets you read and view existing secrets through the CLI, the API and the UI: "You can use the command to read secrets, generate dynamic credentials, get configuration details, and more." Taken literally, the claim that Vault lacks the ability to see existing secrets is false.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The comparison-table row might mean a narrower capability, such as seeing secrets that live in external stores or seeing where secrets are used. The wording should be clarified, because as written it says Vault can't show secrets at all.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports docs say environments can import "configuration and secrets from other environments", and that "The `imports` key is a list of environments that are resolved at runtime." Because imports are resolved each time an environment is opened, a change to the referenced environment shows up in the environments that import it.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs don't say "automatically propagate" in those words; that follows from the runtime-resolution statement. It only holds for unpinned imports. If an import is pinned to a version or tag, later updates would not flow through.

verdicts.text: Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Vault's docs say reads are addressed by path ("The read command reads data from Vault at the given path"). Environments are only a path-naming convention (e.g. kvV2/env/qa, env/dev, env/prod in HashiCorp's own support article), not a first-class object.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Enterprise namespaces could be seen as a scoping construct, but they are tenancy isolation, not a composable environment like ESC's.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports constructing new dynamic values through string interpolation; Vault does not.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC half is Pulumi's own interpolation feature. The flat "Vault does not" is too strong: HashiCorp's docs say Vault Agent's Template feature renders Vault secrets "to files or environment variables ... using Consul Template markup", and that "Agent templates allow you to reformat this data". That lets you build new strings from secret values on the client side. Vault's server-side KV store does not interpolate stored values from other values, so the row is only accurate if it is qualified.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is an absolute "competitor can't" claim. Vault has templating (Agent/Consul Template), but it works differently from ESC's interpolation inside environment definitions. Suggest wording like "Limited — via Vault Agent templates at render time".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source includes `cmd/esc/cli/env_clone.go`, so environments can be cloned (forked). ESC imports also let you layer overrides on an imported environment, which is what the same page's L27 describes: environments "can be composed together from multiple other environments." I didn't check the "Vault has no equivalent" half against Vault's docs, but it fits Vault's path-based KV model.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/contents/cmd/esc/cli (env_clone.go present); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L27
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording is garbled: "without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values" probably means "by importing and overriding specific values", but as written it reads as though overriding is something you avoid.

verdicts.text: `pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault has no equivalent.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source (env_diff.go) defines `diff` with Short "Show changes between versions." and Long "This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." That confirms the Pulumi half. The "Vault has no equivalent" half wasn't checked against HashiCorp docs.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault KV v2 keeps secret versions (`vault kv get -version`) but has no built-in diff command. The "no equivalent" claim is plausible, but it's a negative claim about a competitor that wasn't checked here.

verdicts.text: Vault cannot compare secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Third-party comparisons say Vault has no native environment concept and no built-in diff. Doppler: "Vault also does not provide a visual diffing mechanism for comparing application secrets between environments". Infisical: in Vault "There's no native concept of environments." Both sources are competitors, and neither is official HashiCorp documentation.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim is absolute ("cannot compare"). Users can still compare values by hand by reading separate paths or namespaces. The accurate version is "no built-in cross-environment compare/diff", so consider softening the wording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions including toJSON, fromJSON, fromBase64, and toString.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1 after exhausting its 12-turn cap) The ESC built-in functions reference lists "fn::fromJSON · fn::fromBase64 · fn::join · fn::open · fn::rotate · fn::secret · fn::toBase64 · fn::toJSON · fn::toString". The ESC Go AST package also documents FromBase64/FromJSON ("FromJSON deserializes a JSON string into a value") and ToJSON/ToString expressions.
verdicts.framing_note: Claim says "including", which fits: all four functions it names are a subset of the documented built-in functions.

verdicts.text: Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp docs confirm both examples. Username templating: "Username templating are used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated." Transform secrets engine: it "contains several types of resources that encapsulate different aspects of the information required in order to perform data transformation." The "rather than composing configuration values" part is a comparison. It fits these docs, which describe no general function language for composing config, but no source states it directly.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim cites no source. Both named features exist in HashiCorp's own docs. The contrast with composing config values is the author's reading, not something a source states.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault docs say "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." The pulumi/esc README says "Audit Logging: All actions taken on environments, secrets, or configuration values are fully logged for auditing."
verdicts.framing_note: Small detail: Vault's audit logging is turned off by default and has to be enabled with audit devices. That doesn't contradict the claim that Vault "provides" audit logs.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) None of the public ESC docs I found say secrets are encrypted in transit with TLS or use a unique key per environment at rest. The ESC docs only say fn::secret values are "encrypted at rest and masked in plaintext output". The per-stack key wording ("per-stack encryption key managed by Pulumi Cloud") is from the IaC stack secrets docs, not ESC, so it doesn't prove per-environment keys.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC encryption at rest unique key per environment TLS" and "Pulumi ESC FAQ \"per-environment\" encryption key secrets encrypted"; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/secrets/
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "unique encryption keys per environment" wording may be borrowed from the per-stack key model for IaC secrets. ESC's actual key scheme (per-environment vs. per-org, plus BYOK) needs to be confirmed against product source or the security/FAQ page.

verdicts.text: Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Security Model docs say: "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend. The security barrier automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." Vault's barrier_aes_gcm.go source agrees: it uses a 12-byte nonce and a 256-bit key.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is a near-verbatim paraphrase of HashiCorp's Security Model page.

verdicts.text: Vault's cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and each engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) It's true that Vault's AWS, Azure and GCP secrets engines generate dynamic, short-lived credentials. The claim that every engine is configured with a static credential is wrong. HashiCorp's AWS API docs say: "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)". They also list sourcing credentials from IAM/ECS instance roles. HashiCorp's WIF guidance says "Vault Enterprise supports WIF integration with AWS, Azure, and GCP... without static service accounts."
verdicts.framing_note: A static root credential is the traditional or default setup, but it isn't required. Vault Enterprise can use WIF instead, and the AWS engine can also use ambient instance-role credentials. Suggested fix: say the engines are "typically" configured with a static root credential, or mention WIF.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi pages partly back this up. The UI has an OIDC onboarding flow in the console, and the CLI has `pulumi env setup` ("brings OIDC onboarding to that workflow"). Deployments OIDC can be configured "programmatically with the Pulumi Service provider or via the REST API." I found nothing showing a separate "Pulumi SDK" path. The wording also mixes up two things: Pulumi Cloud acting as the OIDC issuer, and where that trust gets configured.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Used as an OIDC provider from the SDK, CLI, UI" blurs the issuer role with the configuration surfaces. The SDK surface is unconfirmed.

verdicts.text: Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) None of the HashiCorp pages I fetched say whether OIDC provider setup is CLI-only. The docs and tutorials only show CLI/API examples (e.g. `vault write identity/oidc/key/...`). The Vault 1.10 release note says it "moves Vault's OIDC provider functionality to generally available" but says nothing about the UI. I found no passage that confirms or rules out UI support.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran queries "Vault OIDC provider configure UI" and "Vault 1.10 UI OIDC provider configuration..."; https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/identity/oidc-provider; https://groups.google.com/g/hashicorp-announce/c/CusnRk7plDw
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Only available from the CLI" looks doubtful. The HTTP API (identity/oidc/*) and the Terraform provider can also configure it. From memory (not fetched here), recent Vault versions (around 1.11+) also have a UI under Access > OIDC Provider. A reviewer should check the Vault UI docs or changelog.
